en: Oṃ, homage to the Buddha! These ten dharmas lead to the summary of the Mahāyāna, the path of the bodhisattva together with its fruit. What are the ten?
The basis, the mark, the position, the resolute intention, the dwelling, the rebirth, the adoption, the stage, the conduct, and the establishment.
The summary verse:
Support, characteristics, side, intention, and abiding; arising, embracing, stages, conduct, and finally, the foundation.

In that regard, what is the basis? Here, the bodhisattva’s own spiritual lineage (*gotra*), the initial production of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*), and all the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣyā dharmāḥ*) are called the basis. For what reason? Because here—

Having determined the lineage (*gotra*), a bodhisattva must be established [in it], for he is capable of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksambodhi*). Therefore, by virtue of its commonality, the lineage is called the "support" (*ādhāra*). Herein:
Relying upon and established in the first production of the thought of awakening, the bodhisattva applies himself to generosity,
and he also applies himself to ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom; or rather, to the perfections, the accumulation of merit, and the accumulation of knowledge.
And he applies himself to all the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣya-dharma*).

Therefore, the production of the first thought of awakening (*prathama-cittotpāda*) is called the support for the application of the bodhisattva’s conduct. In this regard, the bodhisattva [cultivates] that very...
Relying upon and established in the application of the bodhisattva conduct, one fulfills unexcelled perfect enlightenment; therefore,
that application of the bodhisattva conduct is his [foundation].
It is called the basis for the fulfillment of great enlightenment.

A person who abides in the absence of lineage (agotra-stha), even if they possess the production of the thought of awakening and rely upon effort, is incapable of fulfilling unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. By this [it is shown]:
It should be understood by way of alternative explanation that even for a bodhisattva who has not yet generated the resolve and has not yet engaged in the practice of the bodhisattva conduct,
the lineage (*gotra*) is the support. However, if one who stands in the lineage does not generate the resolve...
One who does not apply oneself to the practices of awakening (bodhicaryā) does not quickly realize awakening; conversely, it should be understood that by doing so, one quickly realizes it.
Furthermore, this lineage (gotra) is called the "basis" (ādhāra).
It is also called the support, the cause, the reliance, the proximate cause, the precursor, and the abode;
just as with the lineage, so too are the first production of the thought of awakening and the entire conduct of a bodhisattva.
In that regard, what is the lineage (*gotra*)? Briefly stated, the lineage is of two kinds:

that which exists by nature (*prakṛtistha*) and that which is acquired through development (*samudānīta*). Among these, the lineage existing by nature is the excellence of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) of bodhisattvas. That...
Such is the lineage that has been transmitted through succession, beginningless in time, and obtained through the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Among these, the acquired lineage (*samudānīta-gotra*) is that which is obtained from the prior cultivation of roots of virtue.
In this context, both types [of lineage] are intended.

Furthermore, that lineage is also called the "seed" (*bīja*), and it is also called the "element" (*dhātu*) or the "nature" (*prakṛti*). Moreover, when its fruit has not yet manifested, it is subtle, being without fruit.
The coarse [nature] is that which has attained its fruit together with the fruit itself;
indeed, by virtue of being endowed with that lineage, Bodhisattvas surpass all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
It should be understood that there is a supreme distinction regarding other beings even before this. Why is that?
Because, in brief, there are these two purifications: purification from the obscuration of afflictions and purification from the obscuration of the knowable.
In that regard,
for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, that lineage, although purified of the obscuration of afflictions,
is further purified by the purification of the obscuration to the knowable.
Therefore, it is called "superior to all" and "unsurpassed.
Furthermore, the distinction of a bodhisattva from śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should be understood through four aspects.
By which four?

By that which is produced by the faculties (*indriya*), by that which is produced by practice (*pratipatti*), by that which is produced by skill (*kauśalya*), and by that which is produced by the fruit (*phala*).
In this regard, this is the distinction produced by the faculties: by their very nature...
The bodhisattva has sharp faculties, the pratyekabuddha has middling faculties, and the śrāvaka has dull faculties.
In this regard, the distinction is based on their practice.
The śrāvaka and the pratyekabuddha are engaged in practice for their own benefit; the bodhisattva, however, is engaged for his own benefit,
for the benefit of others, for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, and for its sake.
For the welfare and happiness of gods and humans,

therein lies this distinction made by skillfulness: both the disciple (śrāvaka) and the solitary buddha (pratyekabuddha) cultivate skillfulness regarding the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, the possible and the impossible, and the truths.
The Bodhisattva [strives] in those and all other fields of knowledge;
herein lies the distinction made by the fruit:
the Śrāvaka attains the fruit of a Śrāvaka’s enlightenment.
A pratyekabuddha attains the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
a bodhisattva attains the fruit of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
These six are the signs of the lineage of the perfections that accrue to a bodhisattva.
By these very signs others recognize, "This is a bodhisattva.

These are the lineage-signs (*gotraliṅga*) of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), and the lineage-signs of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
In this regard, the following is the lineage-sign of a bodhisattva’s perfection of generosity. Here:
A bodhisattva is by nature fond of giving; and when objects to be given are available,
he is constantly and continuously disposed to share them with others, his mind being filled with joy.
He gives without a troubled mind; he is one who practices sharing even from what is little;
he bestows a gift that is pure and not inferior; he feels shame at not giving;
he speaks in praise of giving to others and encourages them toward generosity.
Upon seeing a donor, he becomes joyful and glad of heart;
he rises from his seat and offers a seat to teachers, elders, those worthy of offerings, and those deserving of respect.
Whether asked or unasked, he provides assistance in various matters concerning sentient beings for the sake of their welfare in this world.
In the next world, he provides instruction in justice;
and for those beings terrified by fear of kings, thieves, enemies, water, and so forth,
he provides fearlessness according to his ability.
He protects them from that manifold, extensive, and terrible fear;
he does not misappropriate wealth entrusted to his hand; having received a debt from others, he does not deceive nor does he misappropriate it; he does not [misappropriate] his own inheritance.
He does not deceive nor does he mislead;
regarding various types of articles such as gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, gold, silver, emeralds, musāragalva, lohitikā, and right-spiraling shells,
he correctly awakens one who is deluded and whose mind is perverted, just as he would from any other source.
There would be no deception; how much less would he himself deceive him?
By nature, he is inclined toward noble enjoyments;
his mind inclines toward all noble enjoyments and possessions, and toward noble things.

He is intent upon his professional duties and not on narrow, petty pursuits. Furthermore, there are these calamities in the world, such as addiction to women, addiction to intoxicants, addiction to gambling, and addiction to watching actors, dancers, jesters, and performers; from such calamities as these, he is quickly [withdrawn].
He very quickly attains detachment; he manifests a sense of shame and dread of blame;
and even upon the acquisition of vast enjoyments, he does not become excessively greedy, much less so for small ones. These and others of this kind are [the qualities] of a bodhisattva.
The signs of the lineage of the perfection of generosity are to be understood.
In this regard, these are the signs of the lineage of a bodhisattva’s perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*):
here, a bodhisattva is by nature endowed with actions of body, speech, and mind that are mild, unwholesome, and not excessively fierce.

He does not cause excessive harm to sentient beings; and even after committing a sinful deed, he very quickly attains remorse. Feeling shame for it, he practices accordingly, rather than taking delight in it.
He is by nature one who does not harm sentient beings with hands, clods of earth, sticks, weapons, or the like; he is naturally affectionate and dear to sentient beings,
and [he honors] those worthy of respect at the proper time.

He attends to the elders with the proper conduct of salutation, prostration, rising from his seat, joining his palms, and respectful homage; he is skillful, urbane, compliant with the minds of others, and always preceded by a smile.

He has an open countenance and a pleasant complexion, free from frowning; he is the first to speak. He is grateful and appreciative toward sentient beings who have helped him, and he maintains straightforwardness toward those who seek his assistance.

He does not entice them with deceit or guile; he acquires wealth through righteous means and without violence, not through unrighteous means; by his very nature he desires merit, and he even exerts himself in the meritorious deeds of others.
How much more so for oneself! One is excessively afflicted by the suffering of others—
namely, by seeing or hearing of their execution, imprisonment, mutilation, beating, reviling, threatening, and so forth— and one comes to value the undertaking of the Dharma above all else.
He values the future life;
he perceives danger even in the slightest fault, let alone in a great one; and he provides assistance in the duties and tasks of others, namely:

In agriculture, commerce, cattle-rearing, royal service, writing, calculation, accounting, and the use of seals; in winning over one's master, winning over one's family, winning over the royal court, and winning over friends and enemies; and in the acquisition, preservation, storage, and investment of enjoyments.
He provides assistance in matters such as discharging debts, welcoming and marrying, eating, and communal feasting—
such activities pertaining to the welfare of sentient beings— but he does not participate in quarrels, disputes, conflicts, or litigation, nor in actions intended to harm others.

He restrains them from what ought not to be done— that is, from the ten unwholesome courses of sinful action— which lead to misfortune, harm, and suffering for both himself and others; and he remains under their control.

He becomes subject to the control of others; because of his equal patience and virtue, he sets aside his own business and is employed by others in their own affairs according to their will. Furthermore, his mind becomes tender and gentle, and he is not...
He does not maintain a state of malice or a mind of resentment for long; rather, at that very moment, his mind turns toward amiability.
He holds the truth in high regard and does not deceive others with false words. Not...
Furthermore, he does not take pleasure in, nor does he commit, the sowing of discord among friends;
nor does he speak impulsively words that are incoherent, meaningless, or purposeless;
and he is pleasant-spoken, even toward his own servants and attendants, rather than being harsh.

Moreover, he becomes one who loves the virtues of others and is worthy of proclaiming the true praise of others; these and other similar qualities should be understood as the signs of the lineage of a bodhisattva’s perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
In this regard, these are the signs of the lineage of a bodhisattva’s perfection of patience:
here, a bodhisattva, by his very nature, having received harm from others, does not manifest a mind of malice, nor does he resort to retaliation.
When being conciliated, he quickly accepts the conciliation; he does not harbor resentment, nor does he maintain a long-standing intention of enmity.
These and others of this kind are the qualities of a bodhisattva.
The signs of the lineage for the perfection of patience are to be understood.
In this regard, these are the signs of the lineage of a bodhisattva’s perfection of vigor:
here, a bodhisattva is by nature enterprising; rising early and retiring late, he does not sleep during the day.
He excessively indulges in the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of lying on one's side;
and when a task has arisen, having overcome his laziness and lack of desire to act, he applies himself through careful reflection.
For the sake of accomplishing that task, and in the undertaking of all tasks,
the bodhisattva possesses firm resolve and does not stop until it has been done.
The first production of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) is the primary correct aspiration among all the correct aspirations of a bodhisattva; it subsumes all other correct aspirations.
Therefore, from the very beginning, its intrinsic nature is that of a correct aspiration. Indeed, when that bodhisattva directs his mind toward enlightenment, he forms this mental resolve:
And he utters these words:

"O, may I indeed awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; may I act for the benefit of all sentient beings and establish them in ultimate, final nirvāṇa and in the knowledge of a Tathāgata."

Thus, seeking both his own enlightenment and the welfare of sentient beings, he generates the thought of awakening; therefore, that generation of the thought is characterized by aspiration. Indeed, that...

That production of the thought of enlightenment (cittotpāda) aspires by taking awakening and the welfare of sentient beings as its object; it does not aspire without an object. Therefore, that production of the thought of enlightenment has awakening as its object and the welfare of sentient beings as its object. And that...

The production of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) is wholesome because it is the precursor for gathering all roots of merit conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣya-kuśalamūla*); it is endowed with the quality of supreme skillfulness, auspicious, supremely auspicious, excellent, and supremely excellent; it is the opposite of all misconduct of body, speech, and mind based upon all sentient beings;
and whatever other wholesome things there may be regarding mundane and supramundane goals.
Among all those right aspirations, this right aspiration is the foremost and unsurpassed: namely, the Bodhisattva’s first production of the thought of enlightenment.
Thus, this first production of the thought of awakening should be understood as having five characteristics: by way of its intrinsic nature, its aspect, its object, its qualities, and its excellence.

And from the very moment that bodhicitta arises, the bodhisattva has entered the unsurpassed Great Vehicle of enlightenment; he comes to be designated as a "bodhisattva" by way of conventional linguistic usage. Therefore, he...

The production of the thought of enlightenment is comprised within "entry. Having produced that thought, a bodhisattva gradually attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, but not without having produced it; therefore, it is the cause of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
The production of the thought [of awakening] is the root. And that compassionate bodhisattva, having the intention to protect suffering sentient beings, produces that thought;
therefore, he...

The production of the thought of enlightenment is the natural outflow of compassion; and relying upon and being established in that production of the thought of enlightenment, a bodhisattva [applies himself] to the factors conducive to enlightenment and to the performance of the welfare of sentient beings.

One applies oneself to the training of a bodhisattva; therefore, that production of the thought of enlightenment is the basis for the bodhisattva training. Thus, this first production of the thought of enlightenment is [to be understood] by way of its inclusion, its root, and its natural outflow.
It should also be understood by way of its basis.

Furthermore, that first production of the thought of awakening (bodhicittotpāda) of a bodhisattva is, in brief, of two kinds: leading to deliverance and not leading to deliverance. Among these, that which leads to deliverance is what, once arisen, continues to the very end and never turns back again.

Furthermore, that which is non-leading to liberation is that which, once arisen, does not persist to the end but turns back again. And the turning back of that production of the thought of awakening is also twofold:
absolute and non-absolute. Of these, the absolute...
That which is once turned away from [the world] and does not arise again for the sake of enlightenment is the irreversible [turning away];
whereas that which is turned away but arises again and again for the sake of enlightenment is the non-ultimate [turning away].
Indeed, the arising of that mind should be understood by means of four conditions, four causes, and four powers.
What are the four conditions? Here, a son of good family or a daughter of good family...
He sees the inconceivable and most wonderful miracle and power of a Tathāgata or a Bodhisattva,
or he hears of it from someone who has gained conviction; having seen or heard it, he...
And it occurs thus: "Oh, how great in power is this awakening! For one who stands in it or has set out toward it, such an influence and such a miraculous display as this is seen."
And it is heard that for those bodhisattvas who have thus generated the resolve, the manifestation of such power is precisely this: what is the bodhisattva practice for those bodhisattvas?
In brief, it consists of that wherein bodhisattvas train, that how they train, and that which [they train].
Having condensed all that training into a single whole, it is called the "bodhisattva practice. Furthermore, in what do bodhisattvas train? They train in seven points.
What are the seven points?

They are: one's own welfare, the welfare of others, the meaning of reality, spiritual power, the ripening of sentient beings, the ripening of one's own buddha-qualities, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment as the seventh point.
The Udana:
The welfare of oneself and others, the meaning of reality, spiritual power, the ripening of sentient beings and of one's own buddha-qualities, and seventhly, supreme enlightenment.
What is the welfare of oneself and others? In brief, the welfare of oneself and others should be understood as being of ten kinds:

that which is solitary, that which is connected with others, that which follows from benefit, that which follows from happiness, that which is comprised of causes, that which is comprised of results, that which pertains to this life, that which pertains to future lives, that which is ultimate, and that which is non-ultimate.

In that regard, the purely selfish aim and the purely altruistic aim must be fully understood and abandoned by the bodhisattva, because they transcend the bodhisattva’s discipline and are inconsistent with it;
one should instead train in what remains.

In this regard, this is the purely self-interested aim of a bodhisattva which must be fully understood and abandoned: the pursuit and enjoyment of wealth by one who desires his own happiness, or [the pursuit of wealth] by one who is stingy with the Dharma.
Furthermore, it is the seeking and the upholding of the existent teachings spoken by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; and for one desiring heaven,
the undertaking of morality, the arousal of vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom for the sake of heaven.
[This is] conduct: either the worship of a Tathāgata’s shrine by one who desires the fruits of worldly material things, for the sake of worldly material things;
or, by one desiring gain, [the worship] for the sake of gain, which produces gain, for one's own benefit, and which deceives others.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s benefit for self and others as comprised of cause and fruit?
In brief, it should be understood that there are three kinds of causes and likewise three kinds of fruits:
the ripening cause and the ripening fruit, the merit cause and the merit fruit, and the knowledge cause and the knowledge fruit.
What is maturation (*vipāka*)? In brief, maturation is of eight kinds:
excellence of lifespan, excellence of complexion, excellence of lineage, excellence of sovereignty, being persuasive in speech, great renown, human status, and strength as the eighth.
What is the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*)? Briefly, it is twofold: that which pertains to the suchness (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*) of phenomena, which is the actual nature (*bhūtatā*) of phenomena;
and that which pertains to the full extent (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) of phenomena, which is the totality (*sarvatā*) of phenomena. Thus.
The reality and the totality of all phenomena should be understood as the complete meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*).
Furthermore, that meaning of reality is fourfold according to its different modes:

that which is established by worldly consensus, that which is established by reasoning, that which is the domain of knowledge purified of the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and that which is the domain of knowledge purified of the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

In this regard, for all worldly people, there is a uniformity of vision with respect to a given object through a cognition that has entered into conventional designations, worldly consensus, familiarity, and traditional transmission; for example:
On the earth, this [perception] is of the earth itself, not of fire. As it is on the earth, so it is with respect to fire, water, air, forms, sounds,
odors, tastes, tangibles, food, drink, vehicles, clothing, and the wearing of ornaments.

Regarding household utensils and furnishings, perfumes, garlands, and ointments; regarding dance, song, and instrumental music; regarding light; regarding the attendance of women and men; regarding fields, shops, houses, and property; and regarding pleasure and pain: "This is suffering, not pleasure; this is pleasure, not suffering."

In brief, that object which is the domain of certain conviction— namely, "this is this," "this is not that," "it is thus and not otherwise"— is established by one's own conceptual construction through a conventional designation handed down traditionally among all worldly people. It is not [established by ultimate reality].
Having reflected upon, weighed, and examined it, it is grasped; this is called the reality established by worldly consensus.

What is the reality established through reasoning? It is that which is established by the wise, those learned in the meaning of reason, the discerning, the dialecticians, and the investigators who abide on the level encompassed by reasoning—

relying upon the means of valid cognition consisting of direct perception, inference, and authoritative scripture, based on their own innate intuition, belonging to the stage of ordinary beings, and following the practice of investigation.
In that regard, what is awakening? In brief, awakening is said to consist of two kinds of abandonment and two kinds of knowledge.
In that regard, abandonment is twofold: the abandonment of the obscuration of afflictions and the abandonment of the obscuration of the knowable.
Furthermore, knowledge is twofold, which [arises] from the abandonment of the obscuration of afflictions...

It is stainless knowledge, free from the continuity of all afflictions; and because of the abandonment of the cognitive obscurations, it is the unimpeded and unobstructed knowledge regarding all that is to be known.
Another formulation: pure knowledge, omniscient knowledge, and unimpeded knowledge;
all afflictions and their latent predispositions are the *udāna*.
The nature [of the perfections], all [the perfections], the difficult [perfections],
the universal [perfections], those endowed with human effort, and likewise those of every form.
In brief, this morality consists of nine aspects: it is free from obstacles, endowed with purposefulness, brings happiness in this world and the next, and is likewise pure.
In that regard, what is the ethical discipline (*śīla*) of bodhisattvas? It should be understood as being of nine kinds:

ethical discipline by nature, all-inclusive ethical discipline, difficult ethical discipline, ethical discipline directed in all directions, ethical discipline of a true person, ethical discipline in all its forms, ethical discipline for those who seek relief from distress, ethical discipline for happiness in this and future lives, and pure ethical discipline.
In that regard, what is natural morality (*svabhāva-śīla*)? Briefly, the natural morality of bodhisattvas should be understood as being endowed with four qualities. What are these four?
Through the correct undertaking from others, by means of a perfectly pure intention,

and for one who has transgressed but has generated respect for non-transgression through restoration, the summary should be understood as before, namely as in the Chapter on Ethics (*śīlapaṭala*). It is characterized by the presence of mindfulness.

In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s patience by nature? It is the endurance of the superior, the inferior, and the equal, as well as the endurance of all [persons] and the endurance of everything, whether based on the power of analytical reflection or by way of one's very nature.
Forgiveness with a mind free from worldly desire and through pure compassion—this, in brief, should be understood as the nature of a bodhisattva’s patience (*kṣānti*).
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s complete patience? It should be seen as being of two kinds.
It relies on the side of householders and the side of those who have gone forth. Furthermore, that which relies on both sides should be understood as being threefold:
patience in enduring harm from others, patience in accepting suffering, and patience consisting of resolute conviction through reflection on the Dharma.
In that regard, how does a bodhisattva endure and tolerate harm inflicted by others? Here,
even when confronted with suffering born of harm from others— whether it be intense, continuous, varied, or long-lasting— the bodhisattva trains himself in this way:

"This is the fault of my own actions, by which I myself experience such a fruit of suffering for unwholesome karma committed by my own hand; and yet, I am averse to suffering. Moreover, this lack of patience will lead to it for me once again in the future."

It is the basis for the cause of suffering. Would I then continue to adopt and practice that very phenomenon which constitutes the cause of such suffering? Or rather, would I join myself to that which is undesirable to me by means of my own self?
Therefore, it would be an injury to myself alone, and not so much to others;
for by their very nature, all these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), whether belonging to one's own continuum or that of another, are of the very essence of suffering. Thus, toward others...

Those who, being ignorant, inflict further suffering upon us who are already suffering by nature, it would not be fitting for us— who are wise— to likewise inflict further suffering upon others who are already suffering by nature.
Furthermore, even for the Śrāvakas who are devoted solely to their own welfare, intolerance that produces suffering for both themselves and others would be improper; how much more so, then, for us?

Having reflected upon this, that bodhisattva, being devoted to the welfare of others, cultivates five types of perception and endures all injuries from sentient beings—whether they be friends, enemies, or neutral parties; whether they be inferior, equal, or superior; whether they be happy or suffering; and whether they be endowed with virtues or faults.

What are the five perceptions? They are: the perception of former-life friends, the perception that follows mere phenomena, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, and the perception of possession.
And how does a bodhisattva cultivate the perception of friendliness toward beings who cause harm? Here, a bodhisattva trains himself thus:
"That being is not easily found who has not [been my friend] to me."

After the passing of a long period of time, in previous births, he has been my mother or my father, or my brother or my sister, or my teacher, or my preceptor, or my guru, or one who stood in the place of a guru.
As he attends to this in such a proper manner, the perception of those beings who have done him harm as enemies disappears, and the perception of them as friends becomes established.
Relying upon that perception of them as friends, he endures and forgives their injuries.
And how does a bodhisattva cultivate the perception that follows after mere phenomena regarding sentient beings who cause harm? Here,
a bodhisattva trains himself in this way:
This is merely conditioned formations, merely phenomena, dependent upon conditions. Herein there is no self, no sentient being, no soul,
and no person who could revile, resent, strike, mock, or abuse.
The summary (uddāna) is to be understood as before.
In that regard, what is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a bodhisattva’s vigor?

It should be understood that the intrinsic nature of a bodhisattva’s vigor consists in the bodhisattva’s mental enthusiasm for the gathering of immeasurable wholesome qualities and for acting for the benefit of sentient beings—an enthusiasm that is ardent, uninterrupted, and non-erroneous—as well as the physical, vocal, and mental activity arising therefrom.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s all-inclusive vigor?
Briefly, it should be understood as being of two kinds:
that which relies on the side of the householder and that which relies on the side of the one who has gone forth.
Furthermore, although that [diligence] relies upon both categories, it should be understood as being threefold:
the diligence of armor, the diligence of gathering virtuous qualities, and the diligence for the sake of acting for the benefit of sentient beings.
In this regard, this is the bodhisattva’s diligence of armor:
In this regard, a bodhisattva, even prior to the actual application of the exertion of vigor, first dons the armor of the mind with such enthusiasm:

"If for the sake of liberating even a single sentient being from suffering, I must dwell in the hells—and not in any other state of existence—for as many days and nights as equal a thousand great eons, until the time when bodhisattvas fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, by that very [time] shall it be done.
This is the summary verse (*uddāna*).
Worship with jewels, service to friends, and the final [section] on the immeasurables.
In that regard, what is the Bodhisattva’s worship of the Tathāgatas toward the Tathāgatas?
It should be understood as being, in brief, of ten kinds.

There is worship of the body, worship of a shrine (*caitya*), worship in the presence, worship in the absence, worship performed by oneself, worship caused to be performed by others, worship consisting of gain and honor, sublime worship, unafflicted worship, and worship through practice.
Among these, when a bodhisattva worships the very physical form (*rūpakāya*) of the Tathāgata directly, this is called his "worship of the body.
Among these, when a bodhisattva, with the Tathāgata in mind, worships a stūpa, a temple (*gaha*), a pavilion (*kūṭa*), an ancient shrine, or a new shrine, this is called his "worship of a shrine."
When a bodhisattva worships the body of a Tathāgata or a shrine of a Tathāgata that has appeared before him, directly perceived by his senses, this is called worship in the presence.

In that regard, when a bodhisattva performs face-to-face worship before a Tathāgata or a Tathāgata shrine, he forms a mental state accompanied by such a resolute intention and accompanied by serene faith.
The summary verse is:
"The marvelous and the non-marvelous, equanimity of mind, and being a benefactor."
Likewise, the teaching on requital consists in the state of having unfailing application.
These five marvelous and wonderful qualities of a bodhisattva training in the unsurpassed vehicle of perfect enlightenment should be known.
What are the five?
They are: being affectionate toward all sentient beings without cause.
For the sake of sentient beings alone, there is the endurance of immeasurable suffering within *saṃsāra*;
the knowledge of the skillful means for training those sentient beings who possess many afflictions and are difficult to discipline;
and the penetration into the meaning of reality that is most difficult to understand.
And [fifth] is the possession of inconceivable power.
These five marvelous and wonderful qualities of bodhisattvas are not shared by any other sentient beings.
There are these five non-marvels of a bodhisattva, endowed with which a bodhisattva is said to be "endowed with non-marvelous and wonderful qualities.
What are the five?

That a bodhisattva, being essentially composed of happiness, accepts the entirety of suffering caused by the welfare of others as being itself of the nature of happiness for the sake of benefiting others.

This is the first non-marvelous quality of a bodhisattva, endowed with which a bodhisattva is said to be "endowed with non-marvelous and wonderful qualities. Furthermore, although a bodhisattva knows the faults of saṃsāra and knows the virtues of nirvāṇa, he is nonetheless fond of the purification of sentient beings and finds his very essence in that happiness; thus, he takes the purification of sentient beings as his primary focus.
In this regard, what is the dhāraṇī of the bodhisattvas?
In brief, it should be understood as fourfold:
the dhāraṇī of dharmas, the dhāraṇī of meanings, the dhāraṇī of mantras, and the dhāraṇī for the attainment of the bodhisattva’s patient acceptance (*kṣānti*).
Among these, what is the dhāraṇī of dharmas?

In this regard, a bodhisattva attains such a reinforcement of the power of mindfulness and wisdom that, by the mere act of hearing them, they retain for an immeasurable time immeasurable texts—those not previously memorized, those mastered through verbal recitation, those comprised of collections of names, phrases, and syllables, and those arranged in successive order and connected in sequence.
In that regard, what is the *dhāraṇī* of meaning? It is as before;

however, this is the distinction: one retains for an immeasurable length of time the immeasurable meaning of those very same teachings (*dharma*), which has not been recited and is not familiar to the mind.
In that regard, what is the dhāraṇī of mantras?
Here, a bodhisattva attains such mastery over meditative concentration that those mantra-words which they empower for the sake of pacifying sentient beings become effective.
Supremely perfected and unfailing for the pacification of manifold calamities—
this is called the bodhisattva’s dhāraṇī of mantras.
In that regard, what is the *dhāraṇī* for a bodhisattva to attain the patience of a bodhisattva?

Here, a bodhisattva—who has personally practiced the profound causes, who possesses wisdom, and who dwells in seclusion—does not even utter a word; rather, he perceives those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) which proceed in a continuous stream as being the basis for the three types of suffering: the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of suffering itself (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
In this way, the bodhisattva understands, as it truly is, that all conditioned phenomena are suffering.
Furthermore, regarding all phenomena—both conditioned and unconditioned—the bodhisattva understands their two kinds of selflessness as they truly are:
the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
In this regard, the selflessness of the person is that those existing phenomena are not themselves the person.
Nor does there exist a person (pudgala) other than and separate from existing phenomena (dharma).
In this regard, this is the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya): that within all expressible things, no phenomenon possessing the intrinsic nature of any expression is found.
Thus, a bodhisattva understands, as it truly is, that "all phenomena are without self."

Furthermore, regarding these very conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) whose causes have previously been severed and which subsequently cease without remainder, what are the four kinds of purity in all their aspects?
They are: purity of the basis (*āśraya-śuddhi*), purity of the object (*ālambana-śuddhi*), purity of the mind (*citta-śuddhi*), and purity of knowledge (*jñāna-śuddhi*).

In that regard, what is the purification of the basis (*āśraya-śuddhi*)? It is the complete and ultimate mastery over one’s own personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), characterized by the ability to take up, remain in, or relinquish it at will, through the total and final removal from the basis of all forms of corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to the side of the afflictions (*kleśapakṣya*) along with their latent predispositions (*savāsanā*).
This is called the purification of the basis in all its aspects.

In that regard, what is the purity of the object? It is the mastery over all objects—whether in relation to nirvāṇa, transformation, or manifestation. This is called the purity of the object in all its aspects.
In that regard, what is purity of mind?
As before, it is the purity of mind resulting from the departure of all mental dysfunctions (*cittadauṣṭhulya*) and the accumulation of roots of merit (*kuśalamūla*) in every aspect. All aspects...
This is called the purification of the mind.
In that regard, what is the purification of knowledge?
It is as before: due to the departure of all dysfunctions belonging to the side of ignorance with respect to all objects of knowledge.
Because knowledge is unobstructed, there is mastery over knowledge; this is called the purification of knowledge in all its aspects.

In that regard, what are the ten powers of a Tathāgata? They are: the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*); the power of knowing the ownership of karma (*karmasvaka-jñānabala*); the power of knowing the meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments (*dhyāna-vimokṣa-samādhi-samāpatti-jñānabala*); the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties of beings (*indriya-parāpara-jñānabala*); the power of knowing the various elements (*nānādhātu-jñānabala*); the power of knowing the various inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñānabala*); the power of knowing the paths leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñānabala*); the power of recollecting former abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñānabala*); the power of knowing death and rebirth (*cyutyupapatti-jñānabala*); and the power of knowing the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñānabala*). These are the ten powers of a Tathāgata, as described in the *Daśabala-sūtra*.
They should be understood as explained in detail.
In that regard, whatever has been spoken, uttered, or proclaimed by him is all suchness and not otherwise;
therefore, he is called the Tathāgata. In this context, regarding the fruit—whether auspicious or inauspicious—
That cause which proceeds from reality and is non-deficient is called its locus (*sthāna*), foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*),
support (*niśraya*), and producer (*abhinirvartaka*). That which is a deficient cause for a result that is either pure or impure is called a "non-locus" (*asthāna*) by way of the opposite.
Knowledge free from conceit is said to be "in accordance with reality" (yathābhūta);
it is all-knowing, unattached knowledge, and pure.
